For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

derivations.claim: The relation $\approx_0$ is reflexive because $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, and symmetric by definition. Suppose $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma'\approx_0\Gamma''$. The triangle inequality gives both directed costs between $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma''$ at most zero. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose a finite reverse witness of cost $d<\epsilon$; such witnesses exist because the reverse infimum is zero. Every forward witness of cost $c$ closes with it, so [F2] gives $c+d\ge0$, hence $c>-\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows every forward witness has nonnegative cost and its infimum is at least zero; the same argument reverses the direction. Both infima are therefore zero, proving transitivity. The same argument proves product compatibility: subadditivity makes both product costs at most zero, and any finite reverse witness bounds every forward product witness below by a quantity tending to zero. Positive homogeneity gives scaling compatibility directly. Thus $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling, and the quotient is a commutative monoid.

Reversible splitting [A1] gives accessible transitions in both directions between $(s+t)\Gamma$ and $s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. Extensivity makes each such edge have zero entropy cost. Any reverse witness bounds all forward costs below by [F2]'s closed-cycle inequality, so both infima are zero. Hence $(s+t)\Gamma\approx_0 s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. The empty type $1$ is an identity under composition; its reassociation and permutation identifications have zero cost by the type conventions.

The pair relation $\equiv$ is reflexive using unit catalyst $1$ and symmetric by swapping the two sides. Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via catalyst $C$, and $(A',B')\equiv(A'',B'')$ via catalyst $D$. Their witnesses are
$A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C,\qquad
A'\times B''\times D\approx_0 A''\times B'\times D.$
Multiply the first equivalence by $B''\times D$, the second by $B\times C$, and compose. Reassociating and permuting gives
$A\times B''\times(B'\times C\times D)\approx_0 A''\times B\times(B'\times C\times D),$
which witnesses $(A,B)\equiv(A'',B'')$. Hence $\equiv$ is an equivalence relation.

Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via $C$, so $A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C$. For an arbitrary pair $(D,E)$, multiply this witness by $D\times E$. Reassociation gives $(A\times D)\times(B'\times E)\times C\approx_0(A'\times D)\times(B\times E)\times C$, exactly the witness for $(A\times D,B\times E)\equiv(A'\times D,B'\times E)$. Apply the same argument to a change of representative of $(D,E)$ and use transitivity; addition is representative-independent. Scaling a catalyst witness by $t>0$ and using product compatibility from step 1.1 proves that positive scalar multiplication is representative-independent. Product commutativity and associativity give the additive laws, and the empty type gives $(A\times1,B\times1)=(A,B)$. Swapping a pair gives an inverse: its sum with $(A,B)$ is $(A\times B,B\times A)$, equivalent to $(1,1)$ with unit catalyst because the two product types agree up to permutation and have zero cost in both directions. Thus the classes form an abelian group with zero $[(1,1)]$.

For $t>0$, the displayed operation $t(A,B)=(tA,tB)$ satisfies $t(v+w)=tv+tw$ because scaling distributes over type composition, and $t(sv)=(ts)v$ for $s>0$ by associativity of type scaling. Also $1v=v$. The scalar-addition law for positive $s,t$ follows from step 1.2:
$(s+t)[A,B]=[(s+t)A,(s+t)B]=[sA\times tA,sB\times tB]=s[A,B]+t[A,B].$
The zero scalar is defined as the additive identity, and $(-t)v$ is defined as $t(-v)$, where $-v$ swaps the pair.

The positive scalar laws extend to negative scalars by swapping pairs. For the scalar-addition law with opposite signs, write $s-t$ with $s,t\ge0$. If $s\ge t$, positive scalar addition gives $sv=(s-t)v+tv$, so cancellation in the additive group gives $(s-t)v=sv-tv$; if $t>s$, apply the same identity to $t=(t-s)+s$ and negate. Cases with zero are immediate. For scalar composition, write each nonzero scalar as its sign times a positive magnitude; the defined action swaps the pair once for each negative sign and scales by the product of magnitudes, so $(rs)v=r(sv)$, with zero cases immediate. For distributivity over vector addition, positive scalars distribute by step 4.1 and a negative scalar distributes by taking the additive inverse of that identity. Together with the abelian-group laws in step 3.1, these are all real-vector-space axioms.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of tagged system types closed under finite composition $T\times T'$ and positive scaling $tT$. The entropy $\sigma_T:X_T\to\mathbb R$ is the finite additive extensive entropy from [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]; in particular $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$.

For a decorated closed chain, start with the compound containing every edge input $a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1}$. Apply the edge $a_0\prec b_1$ with all other edge inputs as spectators, then apply $a_1\prec b_2$ with the already produced $b_1$ and all still-unused inputs as spectators, and continue through $a_{N-1}\prec b_N$. Consistency and transitivity give $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}a_k\prec\sum_{k=1}^{N}b_k$. Since $T_N=T_0$ and the intermediate types occur once on each side, these two compounds have the same total type up to the declared reassociation and permutation. Their entropy difference is exactly the chain cost. The same-type entropy representation [F2] makes this difference nonnegative. Hence every closed-chain witness costs at least zero and $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$.

Take finite witnesses for $(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)$ and $(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$. Run the first chain with a fixed state of $\Gamma_2$ and its second catalyst as spectators; then run the second chain with the first chain's output state and first catalyst as spectators. Consistency allows both sequences, and each fixed spectator contributes zero entropy difference. The resulting witness from $\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_2$ to $\Gamma'_1\times\Gamma'_2$ has the sum of the two costs. If both infima are finite real numbers, choose witnesses within $\epsilon/2$ of each infimum and let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. If one infimum is $-\infty$ and the other is finite, use a fixed finite witness for the latter and arbitrarily negative witnesses for the former; the product costs are unbounded below. If both are $-\infty$, choose both costs arbitrarily negative, so the product infimum is $-\infty$. If either is $+\infty$ and the other is not $-\infty$, the right side is $+\infty$ and the inequality is automatic. The mixed extended sum $+\infty+(-\infty)$ is undefined and is excluded by the Statement.

A witness for $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$ is a witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ with enlarged catalyst $C_0\times C$, so $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$. Conversely, add one fixed state of the nonempty catalyst $C_0$ to every edge of an arbitrary witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Its cost is unchanged, proving the reverse inequality. Thus $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$.

Scaling every state, type, and catalyst in a witness by $t>0$ multiplies its cost by $t$ because $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$. This gives $F(t\Gamma,t\Gamma')\le tF(\Gamma,\Gamma')$; applying the same argument with scale $1/t$ gives equality, including the extended values.

Concatenate a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ with one from $\Gamma'$ to $\Gamma''$, adding the other chain's fixed catalyst state as spectator to each edge. The result is a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma''$ whose cost is the sum. Taking finite approximations proves the triangle inequality when both costs are finite; an unbounded-below term with a finite witness in the other direction gives the corresponding $-\infty$ case; if a term is $+\infty$ and the sum is defined, the inequality is automatic. For an actual forward witness and an actual reverse witness with possibly different catalysts, add the reverse catalyst's fixed state to every forward edge and the forward catalyst's fixed state to every reverse edge. Consistency supplies these padded edges, and additivity makes each edge cost unchanged. The padded chains now have the same catalyst, so concatenate them into a closed chain; step 1.1 gives $c+d\ge0$. Thus any fixed finite reverse witness of cost $d$ bounds every forward witness below by $-d$.

Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. derivations.claim: For $0\le\lambda<\mu\le1$, the signed difference $R_\mu-R_\lambda=(\mu-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$ has positive part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and negative part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_0)$. Since $x_0\prec x_1$, positive scaling and [F2] give $R_\lambda\prec R_\mu$. A reverse comparison would, by [F2] and inverse positive scaling, give $x_1\prec x_0$, contrary to strictness. Thus the reference states are strictly ordered by parameter.

For $0<\lambda<1$, [F1] makes $(1-\lambda)x_0$ and $\lambda x_1$ thermally equivalent. By the definition of thermal equivalence, their compound is reversible with its join state. The equal-state split makes $((1-\lambda)x,\lambda x)$ reversible with its join state and with $x$. Both join states belong to the join of two scaled copies of the same simple domain, so [F3] compares them. The endpoint cases use $R_0=x_0$ and $R_1=x_1$ directly. Hence $R_\lambda$ and $x$ are comparable for every $\lambda\in[0,1]$.

Let $L=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:R_\lambda\prec x\}$. The strict endpoint comparison $x_0\prec x$ puts $0$ in $L$. Step 1.1 and transitivity make $L$ downward closed. Let $s=\sup L$. If $s>0$, then $s-1/n\in L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Since $R_{s-1/n}+(1/n)x_1=R_s+(1/n)x_0$, consistency yields $R_s+(1/n)x_0\prec x+(1/n)x_1$. Stability with bases $R_s,x$ and fixed spectators $x_0,x_1$ gives $R_s\prec x$. If $s=0$, this comparison is the given $x_0\prec x$.

If $s<1$, then $s+1/n\notin L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Step 1.2 gives comparability and the definition of $L$ excludes $R_{s+1/n}\prec x$, so $x\prec R_{s+1/n}$. The identity $R_{s+1/n}+(1/n)x_0=R_s+(1/n)x_1$ and stability yield $x\prec R_s$. If $s=1$, the strict strip gives $x\prec R_1$; together with step 2.1 this would imply $x_1\prec x$, contrary to $x\prec\prec x_1$. Thus $s<1$, and step 2.1 and the preceding stability comparison give $R_s\sim x$.

The equivalence $R_s\sim x$ also excludes $s=0$, because $R_0=x_0$ and $x_0\not\sim x$, and excludes $s=1$ by strictness of $x\prec\prec x_1$. If $R_t\sim x$ for another $t$, transitivity gives $R_s\sim R_t$; step 1.1 then forces $s=t$. Hence the parameter is unique and lies in $(0,1)$.

The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$. Its relative interior $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is the interior in $H=\operatorname{aff}C$. Then $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is nonempty. If $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$, $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, and $0\le t<1$, then $(1-t)w+ty\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$.

derivations.claim: Suppose $A_x$ has empty ambient interior. If $d=1$, S1 supplies a strict successor $y\ne x$; convexity puts the nondegenerate interval between $x$ and $y$ in $A_x$, contradicting empty interior. Thus take $d\ge2$. The affine hull of $A_x$ has dimension at most $d-1$. If its dimension were at most $d-2$, [F2] would give two distinct supporting hyperplanes at $x$, contradicting S2. Hence its affine hull is a hyperplane $H$; this $H$ supports $A_x$ at every point, including $x$.

By S1 choose $y$ with $x\prec\prec y$. Then $y\in A_x$ and $x\notin A_y$. Transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x\subseteq H$. If $A_y$ had affine dimension at most $d-2$, [F2] would again give multiple ambient supports at $y$, contrary to S2. Thus $\operatorname{aff}A_y=H$.

Choose $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H A_y$ by [F3]. The segment from $w$ to $x$ is contained in $H\cap\Gamma_i$ by convexity of both sets, starts in $A_y$, and ends outside $A_y$. Its intersection with $A_y$ is closed by relative closedness [F1], so it has a last point $z$ before $x$. Points immediately after $z$ on this segment lie outside $A_y$ and, because $A_y$ is closed in the open set $\Gamma_i$, outside $\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. Thus $z\in\partial_H\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. The support statement [F2] supplies a nonzero functional on $H$ whose zero hyperplane supports $A_y$ at $z$.

Extend this functional to the ambient Euclidean space by taking its normal vector in the direction space of $H$. Its zero hyperplane contains the within-$H$ support and is not $H$ itself. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y$, so the extended plane supports $A_z$ at $z$; the plane $H$ also supports $A_z$. These are distinct, contradicting S2 at $z$. Therefore $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior.

citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

Assume [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and T1–T4 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] for every finite join. For any one simple type $\Gamma_i$, every two finite compounds of its scaled copies with the same total coefficient mass are comparable. Thus CH holds on all multiple scaled products of that type. No entropy across different material types is asserted here.

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.

Let a family of simple domains satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and suppose every pair has an admitted simple thermal join satisfying T1 and T2 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then the fixed-work orientation signs from [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]] agree throughout the family. One common affine proof-coordinate convention $u'=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, therefore makes each fixed-work accessibility order increase with $u'$ and preserves the energy-sum formula for joins. This is a mathematical coordinate convention; it does not change a physical energy quantity or assert a sign of a measured temperature.

derivations.claim: Use [F7]'s common mathematical energy orientation for the proof coordinates. Apply [F2] using [F1] after dividing represented coefficient maps by the fixed positive type weight $w_\Gamma$, as specified in [A1]. Multiply the resulting unit-state entropy by $w_\Gamma$ to evaluate represented states; this positive factor preserves all same-type order comparisons. Write $S(x)$ for that represented-state value. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] and additivity imply concavity: for $0<t<1$, accessibility of $(tx,(1-t)y)$ to $tx+(1-t)y$ gives $tS(x)+(1-t)S(y)\le S(tx+(1-t)y)$. By [F3], $S$ is strictly increasing in energy at fixed work coordinate.

Fix a work coordinate $v$ and let $J_v:=\{u:(u,v)\in\Gamma\}$, an open interval. The restriction $s_v(u)=S(u,v)$ is finite, concave, continuous by [F4], and strictly increasing by [F3]. For an interior $u$, concavity makes the right secant slopes nonincreasing as the secant endpoint moves right, and the left secant slopes monotone as the endpoint approaches $u$; hence the one-sided derivative limits $s'_{v,+}(u)$ and $s'_{v,-}(u)$ exist. Choose $a<u<b$ in $J_v$: the secants to $a,b$ bound those limits, so they are finite, and concavity gives $s'_-\ge s'_+$. Monotonicity gives nonnegative slopes. If $s'_+(u)=0$, then for every $z>u$ concavity bounds $(s_v(z)-s_v(u))/(z-u)\le s'_+(u)=0$, contradicting strict increase. Thus $s'_-\ge s'_+>0$. Define $\Theta(u,v)=[1/s'_{v,-}(u),1/s'_{v,+}(u)]$, a nonempty compact interval of positive finite reciprocal slopes.

Suppose the second alternative fails, so each adiabat contains one thermal-equivalence class. By [F1]–[F2], $A_x=\{y:S(y)\ge S(x)\}$. Continuity of $S$ and strict increase in energy at fixed work coordinate imply that every point with $S=\sigma$ has arbitrarily nearby points with larger and smaller entropy; hence each entropy level $E_\sigma=\{x:S(x)=\sigma\}$ is a forward-sector boundary. The supposition makes each $E_\sigma$ lie in one thermal class. Let $R=S(\Gamma)$ and, for each thermal class $C_\alpha$, put $R_\alpha=\{S(x):x\in C_\alpha\}$. These sets partition $R$: two distinct classes cannot share a level under the supposition. The range $R$ is an interval, since any two points of the convex domain are joined by a segment and the continuous entropy takes every intermediate value along it.

Fix $x=(u_1,v_1)$ and $y=(u_2,v_2)$ of this same simple type, and let $U=u_1+u_2$. The admissible energy splits form the open interval $D=\{w:(U-w,v_1)\in\Gamma,\ (w,v_2)\in\Gamma\}$, which contains $u_2$. Define $g(w)=s_{v_1}(U-w)+s_{v_2}(w)$. For the join state $J(x,y)$, T2 gives an admissible split $q$ whose pair is reversible with the join. For every other split $p$, T1 gives $p\prec J(x,y)\prec q$, so $p\prec q$. The pair states $p,q$ are finite compounds of two copies of this same simple type; [F1]–[F2] and their entropy representation therefore give $g(p)\le g(q)$. Thus $q$ maximizes $g$. If the initial split $x,y$ is reversible with the join, it is equivalent to $q$; entropy representation gives equal entropy, so it too maximizes $g$. Conversely, if $u_2$ maximizes $g$, then $g(u_2)=g(q)$, and [F1]–[F2] make the initial pair reversible with $q$; composing with $q\sim J(x,y)$ shows $x\sim_T y$. For a concave function at an interior point, maximality is equivalent to $g'_+(u_2)\le0\le g'_-(u_2)$: right secants are bounded above by the right derivative and left secants below by the left derivative. Here
$g'_+(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,+}(u_2),\qquad
g'_-(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,-}(u_2).$
The two inequalities are exactly $s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)\le s'_{v_2,-}(u_2)$ and $s'_{v_2,+}(u_2)\le s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)$, which say the positive slope intervals intersect; reciprocal reverses their endpoints, so this is equivalent to $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $T_\alpha$ be one thermal class. The compact intervals $\Theta(x)$, $x\in T_\alpha$, pairwise intersect by step 2.1. For any finite subfamily, pairwise intersection implies common intersection: the largest left endpoint is no greater than the smallest right endpoint, since the intervals attaining those two endpoints intersect. Fix $x_0\in T_\alpha$; the sets $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(x_0)$ are closed subsets of the compact interval $\Theta(x_0)$ and have the finite-intersection property. Compactness [F5] gives a common point, so $I_\alpha:=\bigcap_{x\in T_\alpha}\Theta(x)$ is a nonempty compact interval. If distinct classes had intersecting common intervals, representatives $x,y$ would have intersecting $\Theta$ intervals and would be thermally equivalent by step 2.1, a contradiction. Thus the intervals $I_\alpha$ for distinct classes are disjoint and strictly ordered on the real line; use this as the order of the classes.

For each work coordinate $v$, strict continuity of $s_v$ maps the open interval $J_v$ onto an open interval $R_v\subset R$. On $R_v$, the level-to-class map is nondecreasing: as $u$ increases, concavity makes both one-sided slopes nonincreasing, so both endpoints of $\Theta(u,v)$ are nondecreasing. If two such intervals $\Theta$ are disjoint, monotonicity of both endpoints forces the earlier interval to lie strictly below the later one; by step 3.1, this is the class order. The local class maps agree on overlaps of $R_v$ because each entropy level lies in one class. The open intervals $R_v$ cover $R$. Any compact subinterval of $R$ has a finite subcover by these intervals by [F5]; its intersection graph is connected, since otherwise the connected subinterval would be split into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Chaining the local orders through overlaps proves that the class map is nondecreasing on all of $R$.

Fix $\sigma\in R_\alpha$ and $x\in E_\sigma$. T4 gives $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$. Entropy representation gives $S(x_0)<\sigma<S(x_1)$, and their levels belong to the same class $R_\alpha$. The global nondecreasing order from step 4.1 forces every level between them, including an open neighborhood of $\sigma$, into $R_\alpha$. Thus each class set is open in the interval $R$. Since these disjoint open sets partition connected $R$, only one nonempty class exists. Under the supposition, all states are thermally equivalent, proving the dichotomy.

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

Thus $(x,sx)$ is reversible with its join, which by definition is $x\sim_T sx$. The same argument gives $y\sim_T ty$.

Adopt the following axioms for $\prec$ on every declared pair of finite compounds with equal formal mass in [[def-td-scaled-products-and-comparison]]. Initially this covers equal-composition adiabatic accessibility. If a later channel model admits comparisons between distinct composition types, the same axioms apply to those comparisons and all their finite scaled products; no cross-type transition is admitted by this postulate alone. They are assumptions of the operational model, not consequences of the process definition or of energy additivity.

**A1 (reflexivity).** $A\prec A$ for every state $A$.

**A2 (transitivity).** If $A\prec B$ and $B\prec C$, then $A\prec C$.

**A3 (consistency).** If $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every finite spectator compound $C$ for which both endpoint compounds are admitted and the resulting formal masses agree.

**A4 (scaling).** If $A\prec B$, then $\lambda A\prec\lambda B$ for every $\lambda>0$, using the tagged scaling maps of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]].

**A5 (splitting).** For each state $x$, positive $s<t$, and tagged scaled copies of its material, the state $t x$ is accessible in both directions to the separated pair $(s x,(t-s)x)$. This states reversible splitting of an equilibrium preparation into scaled copies, not additivity of arbitrary state functions.

**A6 (stability).** Let $A,B$ have equal formal mass. Let $Z_0,Z_1$ be fixed positive spectator compounds of equal formal mass, and let $\epsilon_n>0$ decrease to zero. If $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\prec B$.

Equality of formal masses in A6 is required so each comparison is defined; equality of composition vectors is not required when a declared model includes cross-type transitions. A6 is a limiting closure assumption on the relation; it does not assert continuity of any physical process or the existence of a limiting apparatus.

For each simple-system chart $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$, $n_i\ge1$, let $x=(u,v)$, with one energy coordinate $u$ and $n_i$ work coordinates $v$. The chart is a nonempty open convex domain. It is written in fixed numerical coordinates; in a physical chart the energy coordinate is measured in joules and each work coordinate retains its declared unit. Adopt these assumptions for every state $x$ and for every thermal join treated as a simple system:

**A7 (convex-combination accessibility).** For $0<t<1$, the separated scaled pair $(t x,(1-t)y)$ is accessible to the chart state $t x+(1-t)y$, whenever these states are in the declared domains.

For each $x$, define its forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$. Adopt:

**S1 (strict successor).** Some $y\in\Gamma_i$ satisfies $x\prec\prec y$.

**S2 (unique finite-slope support).** At $x=(u_x,v_x)$, $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane through $x$, and it can be written
$$
u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0
$$
with finite $P_i(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_i}$. The map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$ is locally Lipschitz: every point has a neighborhood on which one finite Lipschitz constant bounds $\|P_i(x)-P_i(y)\|/\|x-y\|$. A supporting hyperplane means $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets it at $x$.

**S3 (connected relative boundary).** The boundary $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$, taken in the topology relative to $\Gamma_i$, is arcwise connected.

These are explicit adopted conditions. The slope $P_i$ is a geometric support parameter here; no equation identifying it with measured pressure is asserted. In particular, S1–S3 and A7 do not assert comparison hypothesis for products.

Use thermal joins and $\sim_T$ exactly as defined in [[def-td-thermal-join]]. For every ordered pair of simple systems and every admitted finite join, adopt:

**T1 (joining).** $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$.

**T2 (reversible splitting).** Every join state has at least one split into component states at its stated total energy and work coordinates that is reversible to the join state. Also, for every state $x$ and every $0<t<1$, the equal-state scaled split $(t x,(1-t)x)$ is reversible to $x$.

**T3 (thermal-equilibrium transitivity).** If $x\sim_T y$ and $y\sim_T z$ in the model’s declared contact family, then $x\sim_T z$. This requires the model to provide the relevant joined types and identifications.

**T4 (transversality).** For each simple-system state $x$, there are $x_0,x_1$ in that system with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$.

The axioms apply to admitted types and their joins only. T4 is an assumption about the contact relation; it is not a consequence of an equation of state or of a thermometer reading. The stronger range condition T5 is stated separately in [[post-td-universal-thermal-range]], and join coherence C1 is separately stated in [[post-td-equilibrium-join-coherence]].

For two named simple-system types $i,j$ with energy/work coordinates $x=(u_i,v_i)$ and $y=(u_j,v_j)$, a thermal join is the model-declared compound state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ whose energy coordinate is $u_i+u_j$ and whose work coordinates retain the ordered pair $(v_i,v_j)$. Its join domain consists exactly of those tuples $(u,v_i,v_j)$ for which there are $u_i,u_j$ with $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$ in the component domains and $u=u_i+u_j$. This is a tagged join state, distinct from the separated pair $(x,y)$, even when their total coordinates agree. The contact model declares the pair encoding and join encoding to have the same aggregate composition and extends its accessibility relation to these two encodings; the contact axioms specify which such comparisons are admitted.

Write $x\sim_T y$ exactly when the pair $(x,y)$ and its join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ are accessible in both directions under the declared contact operation. Here $\sim_T$ is a relation between states of the two named systems; it is not numerical equality of temperature. Nested joins use only the model’s declared reassociation and permutation identifications. The coordinate sum alone supplies no accessibility comparison.

Adopt **T5 (universal thermal-equilibrium range)**: for every ordered pair of simple systems $i,j$, each state $x$ of $i$, and every work-coordinate point $v_j$ in the projection of the state domain of $j$, there is some state $y=(u_j,v_j)$ of $j$ with $x\sim_T y$, using [[def-td-thermal-join]].

This is a quantified existence assumption for a thermal-equilibrium partner at each permitted work coordinate. It does not define a numerical temperature, assert that all systems possess the same temperature range as a real apparatus, or supply a calibration map and its uncertainty.

Adopt **C1 (equilibrium-join coherence)**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the joined state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each constituent, $J_{ij}(x,y)\sim_T x$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)\sim_T y$, using the model’s declared nested-join identifications.

C1 is an additional postulate of this completed contact branch. The source’s Theorem 4.8 is stated with T1–T4; the local conditional calibrator route uses the constituent-to-join bridge in addition to the stronger T5 range assumption. Neither fact licenses deriving C1 from $u=u_i+u_j$, from T1–T4, or from transitivity alone. The displayed source supports the contact context, not the claim that its bare printed axioms already contain C1.

Let $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ be simple domains in a family of finite thermal joins satisfying A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5, and C1 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $\Gamma_2$ such that

$$(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0).$$

Moreover, for every fixed finite composition of scaled copies of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, any two equal-mass states of that same composition are comparable (CH). The conclusion is conditional on the explicitly stated join-coherence and universal-range assumptions C1 and T5.

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Fix two simple types $i,j$ in the declared family. Give every primitive material its unit amount vector and use the aggregate composition of [[def-td-scaled-products-and-comparison]] for each scaled, separated or joined type $\Gamma$; its sum is $w_\Gamma>0$ unless the type is empty. Construct [F2]'s encoded state and interpretation maps using the physical tagged scaling maps: a raw coefficient $a>0$ at $(\Gamma,x)$ denotes the preparation $(a/w_\Gamma)x$. The map preserves aggregate composition and formal mass, and distinct raw tags remain distinct. The interpretations of $\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(\delta_s x)$ and $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ are the same declared scaled preparation by composition of scaling maps; reflexivity gives reversible transport. When factor coefficients combine or split, [A1]'s reversible-splitting axiom supplies reversibility, so the pullback inherits composition, positive scaling and stability from [A1]. Dividing fixed-type encoded maps by $w_\Gamma$ and scaling back preserves and reflects comparisons, so the one-copy forward sectors and all geometry in [A2] are unchanged. Any common sign chosen in the mathematical orientation deduction is used only for proof coordinates $u'=\varepsilon U$; the physical energy $U$ retains its fixed SI meaning, units and all independently adopted positive-$S_U$ or calibration qualifications. Since the same sign is applied to each component and join proof coordinate, summed-energy identities are preserved. Thus the actual preparation model supplies the exact formal conventions and all order/geometric hypotheses required by [F1].

By [A3], the physical operation [[def-td-thermal-join]] supplies T1–T4 with the same summed-energy coordinates and reversible splitting used in [F1]. Its pair and join retain the same aggregate composition by [[def-td-thermal-join]], so their encoded weights both equal $w_i+w_j$; no mass-one join is compared to an unweighted mass-two pair.

[A4] supplies the separately stated T5 quantifiers for every ordered simple-system pair, and [A5] supplies the separate C1 nested-join equivalence. Thus every premise of [F1], including its two stronger contact inputs, is met on the whole declared join-closed family.

Apply [F1] to this pair $i,j$. Its first conclusion is states $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ with $(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0)$; its second is comparison for every finite separated product made from scaled copies of these two types. This is precisely the stated pairwise conclusion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ be simple domains in a family of finite thermal joins satisfying A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5, and C1 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $\Gamma_2$ such that

$$(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0).$$

Moreover, for every fixed finite composition of scaled copies of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, any two equal-mass states of that same composition are comparable (CH). The conclusion is conditional on the explicitly stated join-coherence and universal-range assumptions C1 and T5.

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

derivations.claim: Use the positive type normalization in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] whenever invoking [F2]; state entropies evaluate represented maps $\mathsf{J}(x)$, and their unit-label entropy density is $S_i(x)/w_{\Gamma_i}$. Apply [F2] to the meter type and choose its entropy $S_m$ so $S_m(z_0)=0$ and $S_m(z_1)=1$. Set the meter reference to $r_m=z_0$, and use [A1] to choose a reference state $r_i$ and one same-type entropy representative for every $i\ne m$. For each $i\ne m$, use [F1] to choose calibrator states $a_i,b_i\in\Gamma_i$ and $c_i,d_i\in\Gamma_m$ such that $a_i\prec\prec b_i$, $c_i\prec\prec d_i$, and $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$; also choose $r_i\in\Gamma_i$. For the meter label set $a_m=c_m=z_0$ and $b_m=d_m=z_1$; the two pairs $(z_0,z_1)$ and $(z_1,z_0)$ are the same two-copy meter compound up to permutation. Write $S_i^0$ for the selected entropy representative, with $S_m^0=S_m$, and put $\Delta_i=S_i^0(b_i)-S_i^0(a_i)>0$ and $\mu_i=S_m(d_i)-S_m(c_i)>0$. Define $S_i(x):=\frac{\mu_i}{\Delta_i}\bigl(S_i^0(x)-S_i^0(r_i)\bigr)$. Then $S_i(r_i)=0$ and $S_i(b_i)-S_i(a_i)=\mu_i$, matching the meter entropy increment across the chosen calibrator endpoints. For $i=m$, $\Delta_m=\mu_m=1$, so this agrees with the fixed meter normalization.

For a finite separated compound $A$ with factors $(t_\ell i_\ell,x_\ell)$, define $S(A):=\sum_\ell t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$. The sum is finite and invariant under reordering; concatenating compounds adds the sums, and scaling every amount by $t>0$ multiplies it by $t$. The explicit-factor convention in the Statement therefore makes $S$ well-defined, additive, and extensive.

Fix a composition with amounts $M_i$ for finitely many labels and let $A,B$ be two states of that same composition. For a state $x$ of type $i$, put
$s_i(x):=\frac{S_i(x)-S_i(a_i)}{\mu_i}.$
The same-type entropy representation and the CH for type $i$ show
$\mathsf{J}(x)\sim_s(1-s_i(x))\mathsf{J}(a_i)+s_i(x)\mathsf{J}(b_i).$
Indeed, the signed difference has total coefficient zero and $S_i$-value zero, so its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy and therefore compare both ways by [F2]. The calibrator relation gives
$(\mathsf{J}(b_i)-\mathsf{J}(a_i))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i))$
by taking the signed difference of $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$ and canceling common terms with [F3]. Add and scale these identities over the finitely many factors of $A$. With
$q_i(A):=\sum_{\ell:\,i_\ell=i}t_\ell s_i(x_\ell),$
the resulting signed map is
$A\sim_s \sum_i M_i \mathsf{J}(a_i)+\sum_i q_i(A)(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i)),$
where the sums range over the finite support of the composition. The same holds for $B$. Since they have the same composition, the reference base cancels, and $B-A$ is signed-equivalent to the finite meter map
$D:=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i)).$
Extend the meter entropy linearly to raw finite signed coefficient maps using density $S_m(z)/w_{\Gamma_m}$ at a meter raw tag $(\Gamma_m,z)$; in particular its value on $\mathsf{J}(z)$ is $S_m(z)$. Then
$S_m(D)=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)\mu_i=S(B)-S(A).$
The positive and negative parts of $D$ have equal mass. If $S(A)\le S(B)$, the same-type entropy representation [F2] for finite meter products gives $D^-\prec D^+$, hence $D$ compares in the forward signed direction. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F3] transfer this to $A\prec B$. Conversely, if $A\prec B$, the same signed equivalences and translation in [F3] give $D^-\prec D^+$. The meter representation in [F2] then forces $S_m(D)=S(B)-S(A)\ge0$. Reversing the entropy inequality gives the reverse comparison. Thus $S$ characterizes every same-composition comparison. Each particular comparison uses only finitely many labels; no infinite sum or uncountable product occurs.

The meter normalization fixes the multiplicative unit. Changing the chosen reference state for type $i$ changes only its additive constant; on a finite compound these constants contribute amount-weighted conserved-type offsets. This proves the stated freedom and completes the construction.
